note: These are this project's working groupings for colour-coding the map, modelled on the section headings of Britannica's 'Papacy' article. They are not an official Vatican classification; the Holy See publishes the sequence of popes but does not divide it into eras.

eras.label: Early Church
eras.britannica_heading: The early papacy: from St. Peter to 590 ce
eras.summary: From St Peter to the late sixth century, the bishops of Rome led a young Church through persecution, the conversion of the empire and the fall of the West. Many are honoured as saints, though records of their lives are often slight.
eras.rationale: Opens with St Peter (roster 1). Ends with Pelagius II (d. 7 Feb 590, roster 63); the boundary is the election of Gregory I in 590, whom the Catholic Encyclopedia (quoting Milman) calls 'the real father of the medieval papacy': he negotiated with the Lombards when Byzantine help failed, sent the mission to England and administered the Church's estates and Rome's civic needs, foreshadowing papal temporal power. Britannica's first section runs 'from St. Peter to 590 ce'. Alternative: Duffy's first chapter, 'Upon this Rock', ends earlier, with Leo the Great (461).

eras.label: Medieval
eras.summary: From Gregory the Great to Boniface VIII, popes became major figures in a Christian Europe, crowning emperors, reforming the Church and calling crusades and councils. The era closes amid a bitter clash with the French crown.
eras.rationale: Opens with Gregory I (elected 590, consecrated 3 Sept 590; roster 64). Ends with Boniface VIII (roster 193): his conflict with Philip IV of France (Clericis laicos 1296, Unam Sanctam 1302), his seizure at Anagni on 7 Sept 1303 and his death on 11 Oct 1303 mark the end of high-medieval papal claims. After the brief pontificate of Benedict XI, Clement V (elected 1305) settled in France and the popes resided at Avignon c. 1309-1377. Britannica: 'from 590 to 1303'. Alternative: Duffy splits this span into 'Between Two Empires' and 'Set Above Nations' (the latter beginning with the Gregorian reform).

eras.label: Renaissance and Reformation
eras.britannica_heading: The Renaissance and Reformation papacy: from 1303 to 1565
eras.summary: From Benedict XI to Pius IV, the papacy lived through the Avignon years, the Great Western Schism, Renaissance splendour and the Protestant Reformation. It ends with the Council of Trent, which set the course of Catholic renewal.
eras.rationale: Opens with Benedict XI (elected Oct 1303; roster 194), the first pope after Boniface VIII's death, on the eve of the Avignon residence (Clement V; c. 1309-1377). Ends with Pius IV (d. 9 Dec 1565; roster 224), who brought the Council of Trent (opened 13 Dec 1545) to its close on 4 Dec 1563 and confirmed its decrees by the bull Benedictus Deus (26 Jan 1564). Britannica: 'from 1303 to 1565'. Alternative: Duffy treats the Renaissance and Reformation in a single chapter, not separated from the late Middle Ages at 1303.

eras.label: Early modern
eras.britannica_heading: The early modern papacy: from 1566 to 1774
eras.summary: From Pius V to Clement XIV, popes put the reforms of Trent into practice and sent missionaries across the world, while Catholic monarchs grew ever more powerful. The era ends with the suppression of the Jesuits in 1773.
eras.rationale: Opens with Pius V (elected 7 Jan 1566; roster 225), who enforced the discipline of Trent (the Tridentine catechism, breviary and missal followed under him; dates of those not confirmed from the fetched CE page). Ends with Clement XIV (d. 22 Sept 1774; roster 249), who under pressure from the Bourbon courts suppressed the Society of Jesus by the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, dated 21 July 1773. Britannica: 'from 1566 to 1774'. Alternative: Duffy's fifth chapter, 'The Pope and the People', begins in 1774.

eras.label: Modern
eras.britannica_heading: The modern papacy: from 1775 to the 21st century
eras.summary: From Pius VI to Leo XIV, the papacy passed through revolution, the loss of the Papal States and two Vatican Councils. Today's popes are spiritual leaders with a worldwide voice, travelling far beyond Rome.
eras.rationale: Opens with Pius VI (elected 15 Feb 1775; roster 250), whose pontificate ran into the French Revolution: he rejected the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1791), was removed from Rome by French forces in Feb 1798 and died in custody at Valence on 29 Aug 1799. Runs to Leo XIV (elected 8 May 2025; roster 267). Britannica: 'from 1775 to the 21st century'. Alternative: Duffy divides this span at 1903 ('The Pope and the People', 1774-1903; 'The Oracles of God', 1903 onward).

intro.text: The pope is the Bishop of Rome. Catholics believe he is the successor of St Peter, the apostle Christ made the rock of his Church and shepherd of his flock. Together with the bishops, who succeed the other apostles, the pope serves the whole Church, and the Catechism calls him the lasting, visible source and foundation of its unity. This map follows that line of bishops of Rome, from Peter to Leo XIV, and the places they came from.

succession.text: In the early centuries the clergy and people of Rome chose their bishop, often with neighbouring bishops and, later, emperors and kings pressing their claims. In 1059 Pope Nicholas II reserved the election to the cardinals. After a vacancy of almost three years, Gregory X created the conclave in 1274: the cardinals are shut in until they agree. Today the rules are set by Universi Dominici Gregis. Cardinals under 80 vote in the Sistine Chapel, a two-thirds majority is needed, and the ballots are burned after voting. Black smoke means no pope yet; white smoke tells the world a pope has been chosen.

saints.text: The Church honours as saints those whose holiness she formally recognises, as models and intercessors. For the first thousand years, saints such as martyred popes were honoured by local veneration approved by bishops, and many appear in the Roman Martyrology without any formal process. The first person known to have been canonized by a pope is St Ulrich of Augsburg, in 993, by John XV. Today a cause passes through four stages: Servant of God, Venerable, Blessed and Saint, with miracles usually required for the last two.

saints_short.text: Early popes are often honoured as saints by ancient tradition rather than formal canonization. Modern causes pass through four stages: Servant of God, Venerable, Blessed and Saint.

eras_note.text: The five colours group the popes into broad eras: the early Church, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance and Reformation, the early modern period and the modern age. The boundaries fall between pontificates, so each pope belongs to one era. These are this project's own groupings, modelled on common historical divisions, not an official classification of the Church.

antipopes.text: An antipope is someone who claimed to be pope in opposition to the one lawfully elected. Older Catholic reference works count about thirty, from Hippolytus in the third century to Felix V in the fifteenth, including rival claimants in the Great Western Schism. This map follows the Vatican's official list of popes, so antipopes are not shown.
